case.label: D
case.text: Run a point-in-time restore on the existing DB cluster to roll the production cluster back to 14:04 in place. Fix: a reader who knows Backtrack (Aurora MySQL only) may think Aurora can rewind in place; the stem says PostgreSQL, so it cannot.

case.label: D
case.text: Amazon DynamoDB with one table per entity. Fix: DynamoDB is fully managed and scales well, but it has no joins and no PostgreSQL SQL, so the stem constraints (joins, existing PostgreSQL tools) exclude it.

case.label: B
case.text: Modify the existing DB cluster to turn on encryption at rest. Fix: attractive because it is the least work, but encryption at rest cannot be turned on for an existing unencrypted cluster; a snapshot restore with a KMS key is needed.

case.label: D
case.text: Lambda plus EventBridge adds and removes replicas on a schedule and the load is a predictable weekday pattern. Fix: it works, but it is custom code and has more operational overhead than a managed Aurora Auto Scaling policy.

case.label: A
case.text: I/O-Optimized with no I/O charges. Fix: it only pays off when I/O is a large share (roughly a quarter) of spend; at 10 percent the higher instance and storage price of I/O-Optimized costs more, and the steady load makes Reserved Instances the better saving.

case.label: D
case.text: Global database with a European secondary as a second writer. Fix: an Aurora global database has a single primary writer; secondary clusters are read-only, with write forwarding sending writes to the primary, so it is not a second writer.

case.label: A
case.text: A pooling service on EC2 would also fix the connection errors. Fix: it adds instances to run, patch and make highly available, so it does not have the least operational overhead compared with managed RDS Proxy.

case.label: B
case.text: Tier 0 on both large replicas and a tier that removes the small replica from failover. Fix: promotion tiers run 0 to 15 and tier 15 is the lowest priority, not removal; equal tiers on the large replicas do not guarantee Availability Zone 2 first.

case.label: D
case.text: A custom endpoint for the two large replicas. Fix: it balances connections, but it leaves the two small replicas unused, and the requirement is all replicas including ones added later.

case.label: C
case.text: Babelfish so PL/SQL runs without changes. Fix: Babelfish for Aurora PostgreSQL adds SQL Server (T-SQL) compatibility, not Oracle PL/SQL.

answers.flag: The term managed failover could be read as the former managed planned failover (which is now the switchover), and option C is the older documented manual recovery for an unplanned outage, so a careful candidate could hesitate between A, C and D; only the least-overhead phrase and the unavailable primary settle it.

case.label: C
case.text: Remove the secondary from the global database and use its cluster endpoint. Fix: this was the documented manual recovery from an unplanned outage and gives write access fast, but it breaks the global database and forces endpoint changes, so more overhead than a managed failover behind the global writer endpoint.

case.label: D
case.text: Aurora Auto Scaling with replicas sharing read and write load. Fix: Aurora Auto Scaling adds only Aurora Replicas, which serve reads, and does not scale the writer, so write spikes are not handled.

case.label: D
case.text: ElastiCache in front of the read replicas. Fix: it lowers read load and staleness for cached items, but the stem asks for replica lag in milliseconds behind one read endpoint, and the option needs application code to fill and expire the cache.

case.label: D
case.text: No change, because the cluster volume already spans zones. Fix: the data survives, but a single-instance cluster must create a new DB instance, which takes longer than the one-minute requirement; the option claim of seconds is wrong.

case.label: A
case.text: A cross-Region Aurora Replica promoted on failure. Fix: that feature belongs to Aurora MySQL (binlog based); Aurora PostgreSQL uses a global database for cross-Region replication with an RPO of seconds.

answers.flag: The label managed failover can be read as the former managed planned failover, which also moves the primary role without data loss while both Regions are healthy, so option B is defensible next to A for a reader who knows the older name.

case.label: B
case.text: A managed failover of the global database to us-west-2 keeping the global writer endpoint. Fix: under older AWS wording, managed planned failover was the no-data-loss move for healthy Regions; today failover is the unplanned path that can lose data, while switchover is the planned path.

case.label: B
case.text: SCT and DMS ongoing replication. Fix: it gives minimal downtime, but same-engine PostgreSQL to Aurora PostgreSQL needs no schema conversion, and it takes more setup than an Aurora read replica.

case.label: D
case.text: Point-in-time restore to a new cluster. Fix: it also returns the data, but it takes longer (new cluster, new endpoint) than Backtrack, which rewinds the same cluster in place.

answers.flag: Only the word durably excludes ElastiCache (option B); a careful candidate could argue that ElastiCache with Multi-AZ replicas and backups is a common durable session store, and the stem cues (single item by ID, no joins, spiky) plus the rejected team-member proposal point to DynamoDB strongly.

case.label: B
case.text: ElastiCache as the only session store. Fix: it is fast and handles millions of requests, but it is in-memory, and the stem requires durable storage, so it should not be the only store.

case.label: C
case.text: Instance endpoints of the large replicas in application settings. Fix: it reaches the two large replicas, but the team adds and removes replicas often, so a hard-coded list needs constant changes; a custom endpoint tracks membership.

case.label: B
case.text: A cross-Region Aurora Replica promoted on failure. Fix: this gives a low RPO for Aurora MySQL, but Aurora PostgreSQL has no such replica; the global database is the PostgreSQL path.

case.label: B
case.text: Aurora Serverless v2 with a capacity range. Fix: it fits variable load, but for a steady, predictable load over 3 years the Reserved Instance discount on provisioned instances costs less.
